problem.statement: Developers maintaining legacy .NET apps cannot determine the correct ownership/disposal pattern for linked CancellationTokenSource objects, since disposing one CTS silently releases resources tied to a linked CTS in ways that contradict their mental model and official docs.

persona.primary: legacy .NET maintainer debugging a production memory leak

context.situation: A maintainer of an older .NET console app found a memory leak rooted in undisposed CancellationTokenSource objects and is trying to work out the real disposal/ownership semantics of linked CTS instances before fixing it.

current_workarounds: Manually analyzed heap/memory dumps to root retained CancellationTokenSource objects
Built a standalone test harness (dotnetfiddle) comparing different dispose orderings across CTS/linked-CTS to infer actual behavior

possible_wedges.offer: A Roslyn-based analyzer/CLI that scans a legacy .NET codebase for CancellationTokenSource and linked-CTS usage and flags ambiguous disposal ownership or missing Dispose calls.
Submit a code snippet or repo link and get a manual audit report identifying CTS/linked-CTS disposal ownership issues and leak risks.
A WPF-based memory-dump viewer add-on that highlights retained CancellationTokenSource chains and traces them back to the owning/linking code path.

risks: Single evidence item (n=1) from a Stack Overflow-style question, not a validated recurring pattern
Commercial intent and commitment signals are near zero (0.05 and 0.0) — this reads as a curiosity/learning question, not a purchase-driven need
The underlying confusion may be fully resolved by a good answer/blog post rather than requiring any tool
No named competing tools or substitutes appear in the evidence, so market awareness and willingness to pay are unknown
Only one persona type (backend/console app maintainer) is represented; unclear if WPF/audit-tooling users share this exact pain

cheapest_experiment.hypothesis: Legacy .NET maintainers debugging CancellationTokenSource-related memory leaks would engage with a free audit offer that explains and flags linked-CTS disposal ownership issues in their own code.
cheapest_experiment.input: A short technical post/landing page (e.g. answering the 'why does disposing a CTS release a linked CTS' question) with a call-to-action to submit a code snippet or repo link for a free disposal-ownership check.
cheapest_experiment.output: Landing page plus a simple submission form for code snippets/repo links.
cheapest_experiment.commitment_event: A visitor submits their own code (snippet or repo link) for the free audit check.
cheapest_experiment.success_threshold: 5+ distinct code submissions within a few weeks of publishing, suggesting this is a recurring pain worth building tooling for.
cheapest_experiment.failure_threshold: 0-1 submissions after reasonable traffic, suggesting this is an isolated curiosity rather than a broad audit-tooling opportunity.
